As discussed in my previous article , the safest and most effective first-line treatment for most eye irritation, including dry eyes, is lubricating eye drops, also known as artificial tears. When selecting a product, it helps to understand the ingredients. Common active ingredients include polyethylene glycol, polyvinyl alcohol, propylene glycol, carboxymethylcellulose, povidone, glycerin, and mineral oil, each designed to support tear function in different ways. This guide is designed to help you better understand these ingredients so you can make informed choices. You may also find it helpful to review these options with your ophthalmologist to determine which products are best for your specific needs. Ingredients in Lubricating Eye Drops The most common eye drops I recommend, especially in Colorado’s dry climate, are lubricating drops, also known as artificial tears. Retinol: The Gold Standard for Wrinkle Reduction If you’ve explored anti-aging skincare, you’ve heard of retinol. Known for boosting collagen and speeding up cell turnover, retinol helps smooth fine lines and improve skin texture. In eye patches, retinol works gently to encourage fresher, firmer skin under the eyes. Since the area is sensitive, the right formulation matters, look for low concentrations balanced with hydrating ingredients to minimize irritation. 2. Hyaluronic Acid: Deep Hydration for Plumper Skin Dehydration is one of the biggest culprits behind fine lines. Enter hyaluronic acid, a powerhouse that attracts and holds up to 1,000 times its weight in water. In eye patches, it infuses the under-eye area with moisture, giving skin a plumper, smoother appearance. Think of it as an instant quencher for tired, creased skin. 3. Peptides: Building Blocks of Youthful Skin Anti-Wrinkle & Firming Eye Gel Patch Hydrate, smooth & refresh tired eyes with our Anti-Wrinkle & Firming Eye Gel Patches, your daily boost for youthful skin. Shop Now Peptides are short chains of amino acids that signal the skin to produce more collagen and elastin, the proteins responsible for firm, youthful skin. Eye patches with peptides are trending for a reason: they not only soften wrinkles but also help strengthen skin over time, making them a smart addition when you use eye patches for skin care as part of your anti-aging routine. 4. Collagen: Restoring Firmness Under the Eyes Collagen is naturally abundant in youthful skin, but its levels decline as we age. Collagen-infused patches can temporarily firm and smooth the under-eye area. While topical collagen doesn’t penetrate deeply, it creates a protective film on the surface and pairs well with other actives like peptides or retinol to enhance results. 5. Niacinamide (Vitamin B3): Smoothing and Brightening Niacinamide is a gentle yet powerful multi-tasker. It improves skin texture, reduces fine lines, and brightens dull under-eyes. It’s also well-tolerated, making niacinamide-infused patches a great option for daily wrinkle care without the risk of irritation. For even better results, consider the best time to use eye patches, many find them most effective when applied in the evening as part of a calming skincare routine. 6. Vitamin C: Antioxidant Protection Against Aging A favorite in anti-aging skincare, vitamin C fights free radicals that speed up skin aging. It also helps stimulate collagen and brighten dark under-eye shadows. Eye patches with vitamin C are ideal if you’re dealing with both fine lines and dullness. Just make sure they’re stabilized formulations, since vitamin C can be sensitive to light and air. 7. Caffeine: De-Puffing and Firming Effect That morning cup of coffee doesn’t just wake you up, caffeine in eye patches does something similar for your skin. It constricts blood vessels, helping reduce puffiness and temporarily firming the area. It’s often combined with hyaluronic acid or peptides, offering a quick pick-me-up for tired eyes. 8. Ceramides: Strengthening the Skin Barrier Healthy skin starts with a strong barrier. Ceramides are natural lipids that keep moisture locked in and protect against environmental stress. Mechanism Inside the biology Sensitive skin is not a single condition but a phenotype produced by three converging mechanisms. Each operates through measurable biological pathways and each responds to specific dermocosmetic interventions. Patients who are told their sensitivity is psychosomatic are usually patients whose mechanisms have not been mapped. The three pathways below sit on decades of published evidence and explain why a calm, minimal routine outperforms an aggressive corrective one. Skin barrier function and TEWL The stratum corneum is the body's primary water-retention layer. Its corneocyte-lipid bilayer — a brick-and-mortar architecture of dead keratinocytes embedded in ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids — controls how much water the skin loses to the environment. Transepidermal water loss (TEWL), measured in grams per square metre per hour, is the standard biophysical marker of barrier integrity. Healthy skin sits around 5–10 g/m²/h; sensitive and reactive skin commonly measures 12–25 g/m²/h or higher. When the barrier thins, two problems compound. Water loss accelerates, leading to tightness, dullness, and flaking. And the lipid mortar that normally blocks irritants from reaching nerve endings becomes permeable, so substances that healthy skin tolerates without notice — surfactants, low-molecular-weight fragrance, ethanol — penetrate to depths where they trigger neurosensory firing. As well as creating an excessively humid environment, masks can cause friction against your skin, which can damage the delicate layers. Skin that has small cracks or tears is more likely to let in bacteria, causing breakouts. Moisturisers help restore your skin’s natural lipid layers, which can offer protection against the increased humidity. A good moisturiser keeps hydration in, as well as boosting your skin’s natural protective layers to combat excess moisture. Keeping your mask on correctly will help you protect your skin, while also helping to protect those around you. First of all, make sure it’s the right size and shape – your mask should extend from your nose to below your chin for maximum effectiveness. Choosing a mask with a flexible wire for moulding around your nose helps stop your glasses from fogging and ensures a better fit, but make sure you’re gentle so it’s not excessively pressing into your skin. Then, the fit. Your mask needs to offer the right amount of tension. Too tight, and your skin will have no room to breathe, as well as having the fabric pressed tightly to your skin creating increased congestion. Too loose and not only is your mask possibly less effective, the increased movement causes friction against your skin, potentially causing damage. Where possible and only when safe to do so, it can help to give your face short breaks to allow it to dry out and breathe. It’s the difference between a routine that actually works and one that looks impressive on the shelf but delivers nothing on your skin. This guide covers exactly that: the combinations that cause problems and why, the science behind ingredient conflicts, how to separate conflicting actives so you can use them all without compromise, and what to do if things have already gone wrong. If you’re still getting started, our guide on how to build your skincare routine is the best place to begin — then come back here once you’re ready to level up your layering strategy. Let’s get into it. Why Ingredient Compatibility Is the Foundation of Effective Skincare Before we name names, it’s worth understanding why ingredient conflicts happen in the first place. Because once you understand the mechanisms, the specific rules in the next section will make intuitive sense — and you’ll be able to think through new combinations on your own, rather than having to memorize a list. There are three primary reasons that skincare ingredients conflict with each other, and they operate through entirely different mechanisms. pH Conflicts: When Ingredients Cancel Each Other Out Every skincare active operates within an optimal pH range — a window of acidity or alkalinity in which its chemical structure is stable, its formula can penetrate the skin, and its active compounds can do what they’re designed to do. Step outside that window, even slightly, and efficacy drops. Step too far outside it, and the ingredient may stop functioning altogether. This is the core of one of the most common layering mistakes in skincare: applying Vitamin C in its pure L-Ascorbic Acid form alongside Retinol. L-Ascorbic Acid — the most potent, most studied form of Vitamin C — has an optimal pH of approximately 2.5 to 3.5. Retinol, by contrast, is most stable and effective at a pH of around 5.5 to 6.0. When you layer these two together, you disrupt both. The acidic Vitamin C destabilizes the Retinol environment, while the presence of a higher-pH product can neutralize the acidic Vitamin C formula. Neither ingredient gets to operate at its best. More on this in the next section. pH isn’t just about efficacy, either. When pH levels are significantly disrupted on the skin’s surface, it can compromise the skin’s own acid mantle — the thin, slightly acidic film that acts as the first line of barrier defense. Disrupt that, and everything else becomes less effective and more irritating. Oxidation: When One Ingredient Destroys Another Some ingredients aren’t just incompatible — they actively break down the molecular structure of other actives. The clearest example of this is Benzoyl Peroxide and Retinol. Benzoyl Peroxide is an oxidizing agent, which is exactly what makes it effective against acne-causing bacteria. But that same oxidizing power doesn’t turn off when it encounters Retinol. It oxidizes the Retinol molecule itself, rendering it chemically inactive. You’re essentially applying one active that cancels out another — and neither the irritation nor the cost of that combination is worth it. Oxidation conflicts are particularly insidious because they’re invisible. Your skin might not react with obvious redness. Instead, you simply don’t see results — and you may wrongly conclude that Retinol “doesn’t work” for your skin, when in reality, it was never getting the chance to work at all. The micelles surround and dissolve makeup, sunscreen, and grime while leaving your skin’s natural moisture intact. That’s why micellar water is so versatile—it can be used as a makeup remover, cleanser, or even a refreshing skin pick-me-up throughout the day. In short, micellar water gently cleanses your skin without stripping it of moisture, leaving your face feeling soft and balanced. How does micellar water work? Micellar water may look (and feel) just like normal water, but there’s actually a powerful science behind it that allows it to double down as a cleanser . Let’s loo k at what is in micellar water and how it works. Surfactants – which are found in micellar water – have one job: cleansing. They typically have two parts – a water-loving or hydrophilic tail and a fat-loving or lipophilic head. In micellar water, molecules of these surfactants come together to form tiny bubble-like particles called “micelles.” When these micelles meet the oil and dirt on your face, they draw and trap these impurities within them. So, when you wipe the micellar water away from your face, these micelles take all the dirt with them, leaving your skin fresh and clean! Yes, you read that rig ht! Micellar water does clean your skin without rinsing . This means your skin barrier remains undisturbed , preventing your skin from getting irritated. The Pore Refiner: Salicylic Acid While not always a lead ingredient in every serum, salicylic acid is a powerful ally against hyperpigmentation, especially PIH from acne. This beta hydroxy acid (BHA) exfoliates the skin’s surface and penetrates into pores, helping to speed up cell turnover and shed pigmented cells more quickly. Studies have shown that salicylic acid peels can significantly improve pigmentation in darker skin tones with minimal irritation. Understanding “Free From” Claims You’ll often see claims on packaging that are just as important as the ingredients inside. These tell you what the product avoids, which is crucial for preventing irritation. Alcohol Free Formula An alcohol free formula means the product doesn’t contain harsh, drying alcohols like denatured or ethyl alcohol. These are often used to make products feel lightweight and dry quickly, but they can strip the skin’s moisture barrier. For a dark spot corrector you use daily, avoiding these ingredients is key to keeping your skin calm and healthy, since irritation can often make dark spots worse. Fragrance Free Formula Similarly, a fragrance free formula is a big plus. Fragrance, whether synthetic or natural, is one of the most common causes of skin irritation and allergic reactions. The Clinique dark spot corrector line is famously 100% fragrance free to minimize this risk. When you’re trying to calm inflammation and fade PIH, skipping potential irritants like fragrance is always a smart move

As discussed in my previous article , the safest and most effective first-line treatment for most eye irritation, including dry eyes, is lubricating eye drops, also known as artificial tears. When selecting a product, it helps to understand the ingredients. Common active ingredients include polyethylene glycol, polyvinyl alcohol, propylene glycol, carboxymethylcellulose, povidone, glycerin, and mineral oil, each designed to support tear function in different ways. This guide is designed to help you better understand these ingredients so you can make informed choices. You may also find it helpful to review these options with your ophthalmologist to determine which products are best for your specific needs. Ingredients in Lubricating Eye Drops The most common eye drops I recommend, especially in Colorado’s dry climate, are lubricating drops, also known as artificial tears. These help restore moisture to the eye, similar to how lotion protects dry skin.
